title: What Germany's medium-term fiscal plan means for Europe
summary_en: Germany's July 2025 medium-term fiscal plan increases defence and infrastructure spending while ostensibly meeting EU fiscal rules — but Darvas, Zettelmeyer and Welslau argue this is achieved through optimistic GDP-growth and inflation assumptions, plus aggressive backloaded adjustment that is not credible. Under realistic forecasts Germany's debt would rise to ~80% of GDP by 2031. The European Commission's endorsement without rigorous scrutiny risks setting a precedent that erodes the framework's credibility.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian fiscal-policy planning (NGM, ÁKK): the German precedent matters because it tests how strictly the EU fiscal framework will be applied to all member states, including Hungary. Hungary as a higher-debt member has stakes in either (a) consistent enforcement (which limits Hungarian fiscal room) or (b) a flexibilised framework along the Darvas et al. lines that gives low-risk countries longer adjustment paths. The paper sketches the second path explicitly.
